title: Google Business Profile for Dealerships: Full Guide
text:
### Choose One Specific Primary Category

Your primary category is the single highest-impact setting on the entire profile. It is the field Google leans on most when deciding which local searches your dealership is eligible to appear in, and it carries far more ranking weight than any secondary category you add.

Select categories that complete the sentence “this business is a,” not “this business has a,” and never use categories purely as keywords.

Set “Used car dealer” as your primary, adding secondaries such as “Car finance and loan company” only where they genuinely apply. Treat the primary as a settled decision. Changing it can unsettle your ranking for weeks while Google re-evaluates which searches your listing belongs in.

In a Whitespark analysis of 1.8 million profiles, businesses with a specific primary category appeared in the top 10 local results 12.5% of the time, against 9.2% for those on a generic category, roughly a 36% higher rate.

“Used car dealer” set as primary, with genuinely applicable secondaries beneath it.

Here are the best Google Business Profile categories for a car dealership.

Google Business Profile categories for car dealerships, from Google’s category list (September 2026).

| Category | When it should be your primary | When it’s a secondary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Used car dealer | Your core business is selling pre-owned vehicles to retail buyers | You are a new-car franchise dealer whose primary reflects the brand or “Car dealer,” but you also sell used inventory |
| Car dealer | You sell both new and used inventory and no narrower term fits | You sell used primarily but want to remain eligible for broader “car dealer” searches |
| Truck dealer | Trucks are the majority of what you stock and sell | You carry trucks alongside cars, but they are not the core of the business |
| Car leasing service | Leasing is your primary transaction model rather than outright sales | You offer lease options, but most volume is financed or cash purchases |
| Car finance and loan company | Financing is a standalone business, not a dealership add-on | You provide in-house or arranged financing on the vehicles you sell |
| Car accessories store | Selling parts and accessories is your core retail business rather than vehicles | You stock accessories alongside sales |
| Car repair and maintenance service | Repair and maintenance is your main business rather than sales | You run a service function, better placed on a separate service profile than as a secondary on your sales profile |

...

### Dealership Photos: What to Upload and How Often

Shoppers judge a used car by its appearance before they call, so your photo library does real conversion work. Upload real shots of your actual lot and cars, not stock or manufacturer press images. Add fresh photos every month, since recency signals an active listing.

Cover the categories buyers and Google both look for:

- Exterior storefront, so shoppers recognise you on arrival
- Lot inventory as it actually stands this month
- Interior showroom
- Your finance office
- Staff on the floor
- Customer delivery moments

All photos should follow Google’s business photo guidelines.

Birdeye’s 2025 State of Google Business Profiles analysis reports that profiles with 15 or more photos consistently saw stronger engagement in clicks, calls, and directions requests. That is a correlation across profiles rather than proof that photos cause calls, but the direction is consistent.
author: Sam Daaz

title: Complete GBP Optimization Guide for Car Dealerships — A3 Brands
text:
Primary category: get this right. Your primary category is the single strongest ranking signal for map pack visibility, according to Whitespark's 2023 Local Search Ranking Factors study. For most dealers:

- ● New and used: "New Car Dealer"
- ● Used only: "Used Car Dealer"
- ● Service-focused: "Auto Repair Shop"

Pick the one that matches your primary revenue. Don't guess. This one field affects every local search you appear in.

Secondary categories: add all that apply. Google allows up to 10 categories. Dealerships should use them. Common secondary categories:

- ● Used Car Dealer (if primary is New)
- ● Auto Repair Shop
- ● Oil Change Service
- ● Tire Shop
- ● Auto Parts Store
- ● Car Leasing Service
- ● Truck Dealer (if applicable)

Every relevant category you add expands the queries where your profile can appear.

...

## Photos and videos that actually help rankings

Google has confirmed that businesses with photos receive 42% more requests for directions and 35% more click-throughs to websites compared to those without (Google, 2024). For dealerships, photos do two things: they signal to Google that your profile is active, and they signal to buyers that your store is real.

### What to upload:

- ● Exterior shots. Front of dealership. Signage clearly visible. Multiple angles. This is what buyers look for when driving to your store.
- ● Interior shots. Showroom floor. Waiting area. Finance office. Buyers want to know what they're walking into.
- ● Team photos. Sales team. Service advisors. Your GM. Real people make the profile feel human. Stock photos do the opposite.
- ● Inventory highlights. New arrivals. Featured models. Special editions. This isn't about selling a specific car, it's about showing Google and buyers that your lot is stocked and active.
- ● Service bays. Lifts, equipment, clean shop floor. Fixed ops searches are high-intent and high-margin. Show the facility.

### Frequency matters.

Upload at least 5 new photos per week. Google tracks upload frequency as an engagement signal. A profile that gets new photos weekly signals an active, operating business. A profile with no uploads in 6 months looks abandoned, because from Google's perspective, it might be.

### Videos work too.

Short walkarounds of new inventory. Service department tours. Quick GM introductions. Keep them under 30 seconds. Google Business Profile supports video uploads directly.

### One rule: no stock photography.

Buyers spot it instantly. Google's image recognition can identify generic stock images. Use real photos of your real store.

...

## Attributes and services checklist

Google gives you two tools most dealers ignore: attributes and services. Both expand the searches where your profile appears.

Attributes are binary markers, yes/no signals about your business. Google uses them to filter search results. When a buyer searches "wheelchair accessible dealership" or "dealership with Wi-Fi," Google checks attributes.

Mark every applicable attribute:

- ● Wheelchair accessible
- ● Wi-Fi available
- ● Restroom available
- ● LGBTQ+ friendly
- ● Women-led (if applicable)
- ● Veteran-led (if applicable)
- ● Identifies as Black-owned / Latino-owned (if applicable)
- ● Appointment required / Walk-ins welcome
- ● Online estimates available

Every checked attribute is a potential search filter match.

Services let you list specific offerings. For dealerships, this means listing every service your shop performs:

- ● Oil change (conventional and synthetic)
- ● Tire rotation
- ● Tire balancing
- ● Wheel alignment
- ● Brake inspection and repair
- ● Battery testing and replacement
- ● State inspection
- ● Emissions testing
- ● Transmission service
- ● Coolant flush
- ● Air conditioning service
- ● Recall repairs
- ● Factory-scheduled maintenance
- ● Detailing

List all of them. Each service you add is a keyword signal to Google. When someone searches "tire rotation near me," Google checks which businesses in the area have "tire rotation" listed as a service. If you didn't add it, you're not in the running.

This takes 15 minutes to complete.
author: Tim Boyle

title: Competitor Map Analysis for Dealerships | GAS.net
text:
Competitor map analysis means looking at the dealerships and repair shops that appear in Google’s map results for your searches, and comparing their profiles with yours. Much of a Business Profile is public: its category, rating, review count, photos and hours. Set side by side, those details often show why one business appears and another does not.

Updated October 6, 2026

You do not choose your competitors on the map. Google does, one search at a time.

The dealer across town may never appear beside you, while a tire shop two blocks away shows up in every service search.

## How to think about it

1. ### Competitors change with the search.

Sales searches, service searches and parts searches each bring a different set of businesses.
2. ### They change with the location.

The three businesses shown downtown are not the three shown twenty miles out.
3. ### Most of what you need is public.

Anyone can see a profile’s category, rating, review count, photos, hours and links.
4. ### Some of it is not.

A competitor’s calls, clicks and direction requests are visible only to that profile’s owners and managers.

...

### Pick the searches

1. Choose three to five searches that matter, across sales and service.
2. Choose three to five places in your market to search from.
3. Use a phone in each place, or a grid rank tracking tool.
2. Step 2

### Record who appears

1. Write down the three map results for each search and place.
2. Count how often each business appears.
3. Note where you appear and where you do not.
3. Step 3

### Compare profiles

1. Open the profiles that appear most often.
2. Record category, rating, review count, the date of the newest review and the newest photo.
3. Put your own profile in the same table.

## What to compare

| Item | Where to see it | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Category | On the profile, under the name | Whether they are matched to the search and you are not |
| Rating and review count | On the profile | How well known and well regarded they appear to Google |
| Newest review | Sort the reviews by newest | Whether customers are still being asked |
| Photos | The photos section | Whether the profile is being kept up |
| Department profiles | Search their name with the word service | Whether they have an entry in service searches. See service department GBP. |
| Distance from each search point | The map | How much of the result is simply location |
| Business name | On the profile | Whether words have been added against Google’s guidelines |

title: Local SEO Benchmarks for Car Dealers: 2026 Report | Flento
text:
#### The benchmark discipline

This report sets operational standards and a repeatable way to compare your dealership with relevant local peers. It combines official platform guidance with Flento’s industry recommendations. Benchmark here means a defined comparison method; the report does not claim observed global averages or an analysed sample of car dealers.

...

Google documents profile eligibility, representation rules and performance definitions. These define what information belongs on the profile and how supported metrics should be interpreted.

#### Industry context

Google documents dealership, department and new-car brand profile arrangements. Used-car dealerships cannot create profiles for each vehicle brand. These representation rules are not observed sales benchmarks or a ranking-effect estimate.

#### Your comparison data

Use your own dealership records and a defined local-peer set to calculate a baseline. Flento’s scorecard, test plan and illustrative calculation are operating tools. They are not measured market findings.

...

### Relevance. Distance. Prominence.

Google documents the core local-ranking factors; Flento applies them to car dealers.

#### The documented factors

Relevance concerns the match between the business and the search. Distance depends on the searcher’s location. Prominence concerns how well known the business is, including links and reviews. Google does not sell a better local ranking or publish precise algorithm weights.

#### Build the right segment

Segment car dealers by the actual operating model, customer need and service scope. Use dealerships with comparable new or used stock and franchise model as a starting point. Record meaningful differences before treating two locations as interchangeable. Make the actual offer understandable and the business information accurate. Compare observations under consistent conditions; a larger service area or a publishing schedule does not establish a guaranteed ranking improvement.

...

Keep dealership and department contact details distinct. Google permits dealership profiles and additional department profiles; new-car dealers may have profiles for each new-car brand sold, while used-car dealers may not have a profile for each used-car brand. Apply the documented naming and category rules, rather than treating every vehicle listing as a separate business.

...

#### Choose useful proof

Useful evidence includes actual vehicles and clear stock and branch identification. Attribute examples accurately and retain permission where people, private premises or client work are involved. A photograph or credential should answer a customer question rather than imply a result the business cannot substantiate.

#### Check before publishing

For a real Business Profile, use photographs of the actual business, products or service. Check accuracy, permission and confidential details. The conceptual image in this report is editorial artwork, not a real customer location or evidence of an outcome.

Sources: Photos and videos, Maps content policies

...

## 4. Peer comparison and measurement

Local Peer Selection

### Compare businesses that answer the same need.

Flento method for defining a relevant comparison group.

#### Match the operating model

Select dealerships with comparable new or used stock and franchise model. Match geography, service mix, customer segment and fulfilment format. Record meaningful differences in availability or scope rather than ranking every business with a similar category against one undifferentiated average.

#### Record inclusion rules

Specify geography, service type, opening or contact model, language and eligible locations before collecting peer observations. Record why each dealership belongs in the set. Exclude duplicates and unrelated formats rather than adjusting the group after seeing the results.

### Collect the visible facts. Keep unknowns visible.

Flento worksheet for comparing your dealership with relevant local peers.

| Subject | Detail | Consideration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity and location | Name, address model and profile URL | Verify eligibility; do not infer ownership from a search result. |
| Service fit | Categories and publicly described offers | Record what is visible, not assumed capacity. |
| Customer proof | Review count, rating and useful imagery | Save collection conditions; these do not reveal completed sales. |
| Action path | Website, phone and supported booking links | Test the destination and record failures. |
| Visibility check | Query, location, language and observed placement | |
| | | Do not label an unobserved result as rank zero.

title: The ultimate Google Business Profile checklist for car dealerships - Localise
text:
To determine which dealerships appear in local searches, Google uses three key factors:

Proximity – How close the searcher is to your dealership

Prominence – Your reputation, reviews, and online authority

Relevance – How well your profile matches what someone is searching for

To influence these, your GBP needs consistent attention across three areas:

Data Management Keep your core information accurate and consistent – this includes your business name, opening hours, website, services, categories, and even linked social profiles.

Optimisations From uploading new photos and sharing offer posts to using keyword-rich content and linking to targeted landing pages – every detail improves visibility.

Reputation Review generation, fast responses, and keyword-aware replies all help signal quality and relevance to Google, boosting your position in local search.

### The Google Business Profile checklist for dealers

Here’s what every dealership should review:

1. Business Information Accuracy Ensure your dealership name, address, phone number, and website are correct and consistent with your website and directories.

2. Categories and Attributes Select the right primary category (e.g., Car Dealer) and relevant secondary categories (e.g., Used Car Dealer, Car Leasing Service). Add attributes like wheelchair access or languages spoken to stand out.

3. Opening Hours (Including Special Hours) Keep your hours up to date – including bank holidays and seasonal changes. Mismatched times frustrate customers and damage trust.

4. High-Quality Photos and Videos Add recent, high-quality images of your showroom, forecourt, and vehicles. Videos showing your facilities, team, or customer handovers can help bring your dealership to life.

5. Products and Services List key offerings – from new and used vehicle listings to servicing, parts, and Motability. Use the Products and Services features to showcase these with descriptions and pricing where appropriate.

6. Regular Posts and Updates Use GBP Posts to share offers, events, or news. Fresh content shows customers (and Google) that your business is active and responsive.

7. Review Management Encourage satisfied customers to leave reviews. More importantly, respond to all reviews – good or bad – in a timely and professional manner. Dedicate some time in your calendar each week towards review management and your GBP will start to shine!
author: Leanna Andrews

title: Car Dealership SEO: The 2026 Local Guide
text:
A fully optimized GBP for a car dealership goes beyond basic business information, it includes inventory signals, service department details, and hours for all departments.

Priority GBP fields for car dealerships:

1. Business name: Dealership name exactly as branded, no extra keywords
2. Primary category: "Car Dealer" for new car dealers; "Used Car Dealer" if that's your primary business
3. Phone number: Main dealership number with local area code
4. Hours: Separate hours for showroom, service department, and parts department if they differ
5. Business description: 750 characters, mention your brands (makes you sell), whether you sell new or used or both, financing availability, and your service department
6. Website: Link to your main dealership site (or separate pages for new and used inventory)
7. Service options: test drives, financing, trade-in appraisals, home delivery if offered

...

## 3. Step 2: Category Selection for Auto Dealers

Category selection for dealerships is more nuanced than most business types, the right categories determine which searches you appear in.

Recommended categories for new car dealerships:

1. Primary: Car Dealer (for general dealership searches)
2. Secondary: [Brand] Dealer (e.g., Toyota Dealer, Ford Dealer, Google has brand-specific categories)
3. Secondary: Used Car Dealer (if you carry a used inventory)
4. Secondary: Auto Parts Store (if you have a parts counter open to the public)
5. Secondary: Car Repair and Maintenance (for your service department visibility)

For used car lots:

1. Primary: Used Car Dealer
2. Secondary: Car Dealer
3. Secondary: Car Finance and Loan Company (if buy-here-pay-here)

💡 Pro Tip: The brand-specific dealer categories (Toyota Dealer, Honda Dealer) are some of the most valuable in local automotive search. Confirm you have your brand's specific category set as a secondary.

...

## 5. Step 4: Use GBP Inventory and Product Features

Google Business Profile's product and service listing features allow car dealerships to showcase inventory directly in the listing, giving buyers a reason to click through.

Adding vehicle models as products in your GBP creates inventory-level visibility. When a buyer searches "Toyota Camry dealer near me," a dealership whose GBP shows a Camry listing has a conversion advantage over one that shows nothing.

How to use GBP products for dealership inventory:

1. Add your top-selling models as products with photos, descriptions, and starting price ranges
2. Update these when models change or inventory shifts
3. Use the service listing feature to showcase your service department offerings: oil change, tire rotation, brake service, these appear in service-specific searches

...

You want inventory signals at both touchpoints.
author: Kevin Reed

title: Google Business Profile for Automotive Businesses | Review Flywheel
text:
| Profile field | What good looks like for automotive businesses | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business name | Your real-world trading name, matching your signage, website and invoices. | Adding “Best Garage”, multiple towns, services or phone numbers to the name. |
| Address or service area | The exact workshop location, or a realistic list of areas you actually visit. | Showing a home address when customers cannot attend, or selecting a huge area you rarely cover. |
| Opening hours | Normal workshop hours plus accurate bank-holiday, Christmas and temporary closure hours. | Leaving “open 24 hours” on a profile when calls are not answered or vehicles cannot be accepted. |
| Telephone number | A direct local business number that reaches the location or booking team. | Using a disconnected number or a tracking number that hides the business identity. |
| Website and booking link | A relevant page where customers can request a repair, book an MOT or enquire about stock. | Sending every visitor to a generic homepage with no obvious next step. |
| Attributes | Only available, truthful details such as applicable payment, access or amenity options. | Assuming every possible attribute is available to every automotive category. |

...

### Choose a primary category that describes the core business

Your primary category should describe what the business principally is, not every job it can undertake. A general independent workshop might use a category such as “Auto repair shop”; a business chiefly selling used cars may be better represented by a dealer category; a specialist tyre business should favour the appropriate tyre category where it is available.

Add secondary categories only where they reflect substantial, genuine parts of the business. For example, a garage with a properly operated MOT testing function and tyre fitting might add relevant categories if offered in the category selector. Do not add categories for work you occasionally outsource or do not provide. Category options vary by country and change over time, so use the current options offered in the profile rather than copying a competitor’s list.

...

## Turn automotive services into clear customer choices

The services editor can help eligible businesses show the work they provide. Google says services may be highlighted when a local customer searches for an offering, and businesses can add custom services where appropriate. Review how the services editor works.

Use customer language and separate broad service types into recognisable jobs. This improves clarity for people comparing businesses and makes the profile easier to maintain.

### Do

- List services you deliver yourself, such as interim servicing, full servicing, brake repairs, wheel alignment, diagnostics or vehicle recovery.
- Use clear names: “MOT test”, “air conditioning service”, “DPF diagnostics” or “mobile battery replacement”.
- Add concise descriptions where the customer needs context, such as what is included in a pre-purchase inspection.
- Review service entries quarterly as your equipment, staffing or specialisms change.

...

## Use photos to reduce uncertainty before the visit

Automotive customers want to see that a business is real, findable and equipped for the job. Google recommends authentic, well-lit, in-focus images and says exterior photographs can help customers recognise the business when they arrive. Its published technical guidance recommends JPG or PNG files, generally between 10 KB and 5 MB, with a recommended resolution of 720 × 720 pixels. Read Google’s current photo and video requirements.

### Automotive photo checklist

- Exterior signage, entrance, customer parking and a recognisable approach to the premises.
- Reception, waiting area and accessible facilities where relevant.
- Clean, safely presented workshop bays, ramps, diagnostic equipment and tyre equipment.
- Team members at work, with consent and sensible safety practice visible.
- Examples of the types of vehicles or work you handle, without revealing number plates, personal documents or customer details unnecessarily.
- For dealers, representative stock and the forecourt — not misleading archive imagery.
- Fresh images added when signage, premises, staff presentation or key equipment changes.

Avoid heavily filtered stock images, photos that obscure the business identity and images showing unsafe workshop behaviour. The goal is not a perfect catalogue: it is credible visual proof that reassures a driver before they travel.
author: ReviewFlywheel

title: [Auto Edition] Nested Case Study: Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep, Ram
text:
### The Experiment

1. Nested Departments Setup – Separate Google Business Profiles were created for the Service department, Parts, Tire Center, Oil Change Service, Brake Shop, Transmission Shop, and Auto Air Conditioning Repair, and we connected them under the main Safford Brown CDJR Sterling listing. 
2. Profile Optimization – Each department was created with optimized categories, business description, attributes/services, and more. 
3. Content Updates – New photos and posts were added for each department to improve engagement and freshness. 
4. Review Engagement – Responses to customer reviews enhanced trust signals and local search relevance. 

The full setup was completed in just five days, making implementation fast and efficient.

...

### Results

The experiment began in mid-August, and within just five days, a noticeable lift in driving directions was already evident. Despite starting on August 14, the dealership gained an additional 98 directions in that partial month. In the first full month after implementing nested departments, driving directions increased significantly: building on the 557 directions from the existing sales profile, we observed:

- Sales: +1 driving directions 
- Service: +35 driving directions 
- Parts: +70 driving directions 
- Tire Shop: +57 driving directions 
- Auto Air: +27 driving directions 
- Break Shop: +48 driving directions 
- Transmission: +54 driving directions 
- Oil Change: +51 driving directions 
- Overall:+343 driving directions across all newly created and nested departments 

- That is a 61% increase in the first full month.

Continuous Growth: 

- Expanded Driving Directions: Safford Brown CDJR Sterling saw an additional +828 driving directions between 8/14 and 11/10 from their new listings alone. 
- Average Foot Traffic Increase:+29% across all locations

Each department captured additional searches, demonstrating that nested listings can expand visibility and engagement without affecting the main dealership profile.
author: Luke Waldschmidt

title: skills/dealer-gbp-audit/SKILL.md
text:
A 10-dimension, 100-point audit of a car dealership's Google Business Profile (GBP), the single highest-leverage local SEO surface for a franchise or independent dealer. The Google local pack and Google Maps drive a disproportionate share of dealer phone calls and direction requests, and a misconfigured or under-optimized GBP suppresses both even when the dealer's website is healthy.

This skill diagnoses the GBP across categories, NAP consistency, hours of operation, services and attributes, photos and visual freshness, posts and engagement, Q&A, review velocity and signal, review response discipline, and dealer-group multi-rooftop consistency.

...

## What this audits

Ten dimensions, 100 points total:

1. **Primary category accuracy** — 12 pts
2. **Secondary categories** — 8 pts
3. **NAP consistency (Name, Address, Phone)** — 10 pts
4. **Hours of operation** — 8 pts
5. **Services list** — 10 pts
6. **Attributes** — 7 pts
7. **Photos and visual freshness** — 12 pts
8. **Posts and engagement** — 8 pts
9. **Q&A management** — 10 pts
10. **Review signal and response discipline** — 15 pts

Multi-rooftop dealer groups receive an additional overlay assessing cross-location consistency.

...

### Mode B. Public-search audit (competitor or no-access scenario)

If the user does not have GBP manager access (auditing a competitor or a prospect), run the entire audit from public Google Search and Google Maps. Many dimensions are visible publicly: primary category (shown in Search), NAP (shown in Search and Maps), hours, photos, posts, Q&A, reviews, and response patterns. Attributes and services are partially visible. Mark any non-public dimension as "verification required."
